title: What are the ways to read a very large text file in Java and their trade-offs: `Scanner` is slow (avoid for big files); `BufferedReader.readLine()` is the simple memory-friendly baseline; `Files.lines(path)` gives a lazy, streaming `Stream<String>` (must be closed: it holds a file handle); low-level `FileChannel` + `ByteBuffer` or a `MappedByteBuffer` (memory-mapped) are fastest for huge files but require manual byte→text handling: and what is the ONE rule that matters most regardless of API (STREAM/process line-by-line or in bounded chunks, never load the whole file into a `List`/`String` in memory, or you risk an `OutOfMemoryError`)?
shortTitle: What are the ways to read a very large text file in Java, and their trade-offs?
keyPoints: Scanner is convenient but slow for large files because of regex parsing and synchronization overhead.
BufferedReader.readLine() is the simple, memory-friendly baseline that keeps only the current line plus an internal buffer in memory.
Files.lines(path) returns a lazy Stream of lines that must be closed because it holds an open file handle.
FileChannel with ByteBuffer or MappedByteBuffer is fastest for huge files but requires manual byte-to-text decoding and line splitting.
Never use Files.readAllLines() or Files.readString() on large files because they load everything into memory and risk OutOfMemoryError.
Always specify the charset explicitly (StandardCharsets.UTF_8) rather than relying on the platform default.
The one rule: process line-by-line or in bounded chunks and reduce to a bounded result as you go.

s1_definition.oneliner: Pick BufferedReader or Files.lines for simple streaming, FileChannel or mapping for maximum speed, but above all stream line-by-line and never load the whole file into memory.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **`Scanner`** – convenient but slow for big files due to regex delimiter parsing and internal synchronization.
- **`BufferedReader.readLine()`** – the memory-friendly baseline; reads one line at a time through a reusable internal buffer.
- **`Files.lines(path)`** – returns a lazy `Stream<String>` that reads on demand; must be closed because it holds an open file handle.
- **`FileChannel` + `ByteBuffer`** – reads raw bytes into a reusable buffer for maximum throughput; requires manual charset decoding.
- **`MappedByteBuffer`** – memory-maps file pages for zero-copy access; fastest but lowest-level.
- **The one rule** – process incrementally and never accumulate the whole file into a `List` or `String`.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India must process a transaction file with a hundred million lines. Loading the whole file is like trying to carry every ledger book at once – you collapse with an OutOfMemoryError. BufferedReader is a steady clerk handing you one line at a time. Files.lines is a conveyor belt delivering lines on demand, but you must switch it off when done. FileChannel is a forklift moving raw pallets – fastest for huge loads, but you must unpack them yourself.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Large File (10 GB)
       │
       ├──▶ Files.readAllLines()  ──▶ List<String> in heap ──▶ OOM!
       │
       ├──▶ Scanner              ──▶ line-by-line (slow, regex)
       │
       ├──▶ BufferedReader       ──▶ line-by-line (fast, simple)
       │         │
       │         └── buffer (8 KB) + current line in memory
       │
       ├──▶ Files.lines()        ──▶ lazy Stream<String>
       │         │
       │         └── MUST close (holds file handle)
       │
       └──▶ FileChannel/Mapped   ──▶ raw bytes (fastest)
                 │
                 └── manual decode + line split
```

```text
  The One Rule:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Process line-by-line or in chunks.     │
  │  Reduce to a bounded result as you go.  │
  │  NEVER load the whole file into memory. │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
There are several ways to read a very large text file in Java, and the choice is about speed versus simplicity. `Scanner` is convenient but slow for big files because of regex parsing. `BufferedReader.readLine()` is the simple, memory-friendly baseline that keeps only the current line and a small buffer in memory. `Files.lines()` gives a lazy stream that reads on demand and lets you filter and reduce expressively, but it holds an open file handle so you must always close it with try-with-resources. `FileChannel` and `MappedByteBuffer` are fastest because the OS pages data with no system call overhead, but they force you to decode bytes and split lines manually.

The one rule that dominates all API choices is to process incrementally. Stream line-by-line or in bounded chunks and reduce to a bounded result as you go. Never load the whole file into a `List` or a `String`, because that makes memory grow with file size and guarantees an `OutOfMemoryError` on a large enough input.

In banking at National Bank of India, Rajesh's first version of a daily reconciliation script used `Files.readAllLines()` and crashed in production with an `OutOfMemoryError` on a fifty-million-line file. Pankaj rewrote it to stream with `BufferedReader`, keeping only a running `BigDecimal` total per account, and it ran comfortably in a tiny heap. For the reporting dashboard, `Files.lines()` inside try-with-resources reduced to a single total rather than collecting.

Remember one sentence: the API is a performance choice, but streaming line-by-line is a correctness requirement that prevents `OutOfMemoryError` on any file size.
